sources.title: RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

beats.goal: The learner knows JSON is plain text that describes data.
beats.content: JSON is a text format for data. A JSON document is one value. A value is one of six types: an object (name/value pairs in curly braces), an array (an ordered list in square brackets), a string (in double quotes), a number, true or false, or null.
beats.question: Before we go on: which of these do you think is a string in JSON, 42 or "42"? Why?

beats.goal: The learner knows the rules that trip people up.
beats.content: JSON is stricter than JavaScript. Names in objects must be strings in double quotes. Single quotes are not allowed. A trailing comma after the last item is an error. There are no comments.
beats.question: Predict: is {"port": 8080,} valid JSON? What would a parser say?

checkpoint.question: In your own words: what is the difference between {"port": 8080} and {"port": "8080"}, and why might a program care?
checkpoint.rubric: A good answer says the first value is a number and the second is a string, and that a program reading the value may compare, add or validate it differently (for example, a server expecting a number may reject or mishandle a string). Exact wording does not matter.

branches.when: The answer identifies number versus string and gives any sensible reason a program might care.
branches.message: You can tell the types apart. Next, a config file an AI wrote, with one planted bug.

branches.when: The answer misses the number/string difference or gives no reason it matters.
branches.message: Let's go over the six value types once more before moving on.
